lesson.title: append(): Growing a List One Item at a Time
lesson.summary: A close look at .append(), which adds a single element to the end of a list in place and always returns None, and the accumulator pattern it powers.
lesson.body:
Of all the list methods, append is the one you will reach for most often, because it captures the simplest possible way to grow a collection: put one more thing on the end. As you learned in the List Methods overview, append mutates the list it is called on directly and returns None, so its entire effect is the side effect of adding an item; there is nothing to catch in a variable.

The syntax is list.append(item), where item becomes the new final element. It is worth being precise about what "one element" means here: append always adds exactly the object you give it as a single new slot in the list, even if that object is itself a list. It never looks inside what you pass in and merges it element by element; it just tacks it on whole.

squares = []
for n in range(1, 6):
    squares.append(n ** 2)
print(squares)

squares.append([100, 121])
print(squares)

Trace the loop first. squares starts empty. On each pass, n takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in turn, and n ** 2 computes 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 respectively, with each result appended immediately. After the loop finishes, squares holds [1, 4, 9, 16, 25], which is exactly what the first print shows. This is the accumulator pattern from loops and recursion made concrete: start with an empty container, repeat an action, and append one new piece of the answer each time through.

The second call, squares.append([100, 121]), adds the two-element list [100, 121] as a single new item, not as two separate new items. The result is [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, [100, 121]], a list of six elements where the sixth element happens to be another list. This nesting behavior surprises a lot of beginners who expect append to flatten things automatically; it never does. If you ever do want to merge every element of another sequence in individually, that calls for a different method entirely (Python's extend), but that is a separate tool from append and outside what this concept covers.

Because append only ever adds to the end, and Python lists are built to grow efficiently there, append is a fast, roughly constant-time operation regardless of list length, which matters once you start building large lists inside loops.

Remember the trap from the previous concept: append returns None, always. If a list variable mysteriously becomes None, look for a line like my_list = my_list.append(something) and drop the reassignment; the append call alone was already doing everything you needed.

Append also interacts with mutability, especially once you pass a list into a function. Because a list is mutable and Python passes it by reference rather than by copying it, a function that calls append on a parameter changes the original list the caller passed in, not a private copy.

def add_bonus(scores):
    scores.append(100)

grades = [88, 92, 79]
add_bonus(grades)
print(grades)

Here scores inside the function and grades outside it are two different names for the exact same list object, just as alias and original were in the mutability concept. When the function calls scores.append(100), it mutates that shared object directly, so grades has changed by the time the function returns, even though grades itself never appeared inside the function body. print(grades) shows [88, 92, 79, 100]. This can be useful design, letting a function update a caller's data without returning anything, but it can also cause subtle bugs when a function changes data the caller did not expect to be touched.
